newsitem.title: UK: London Exchange sets out rules for new market.
newsitem.headline: London Exchange sets out rules for new market.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange on Friday laid out proposed rules for the new order-driven market planned to be introduced next year, confirming that brokerages will be allowed to delay reporting of some large trades.
Following feedback on proposals originally published in October, the Exchange said it had revised its proposals to reflect the needs of different users of the market.
"The structure needs to balance the interests of private investors, institutional investors and intermediaries wishing to transact large trades," the Exchange said.
"The rules have been designed to meet their differing needs and to provide a liquid, transparent and viable market structure."
It said the new rules would still mean that some 75 percent of trades by value and 95 percent by volume would be published immediately -- the same proportion as under the present system.
The Exchange said the new rules "represent an evolutionary approach which should...ensure both a high level of transparency and a liquid order book."

Under the original proposals in October, all trades would have had to be published immediately. Yet some major brokerages were reported this week to have objected to this idea on the grounds that it could have compromised their trading positions.
The new proposal states that reporting of trades which are greater than six times the normal market size in a specific stock can be delayed by up to 60 minutes.
It said this revision "addresses concerns that the original proposal would damage liquidity and the ability to commit risk capital."

The proposals state that large risk trades need not interact with the on-screen order book, and that 15-minute suspensions will be introduced if a stock price moves five percent or more from the opening price or from its last suspension price.

The move to order-driven trading, planned for October 20 next year, has been the subject of intense debate in the London securities industry this year, with some major firms initially opposing the change on grounds that it would sap liquidity.
The dispute was at the heart of the row which led to the departure of the Exchange's chief executive Michael Lawrence in January.

Since then even hard-line brokerages have come round to accepting the transition to the new market, which will replace the current system of traders quoting prices on screen and agreeing deals by phone.
However the detailed operation of the new market remains
controversial, with some claiming that the Exchange's largest members are still able to twist the rules to suit their purposes.
The Exchange said the market had until January 10 to respond to the proposals.
